result:
There is a strange kind of freedom in being told to "write freely." No prompt, no constraints, no box to fit inside. Just - go. For 2500 words, just exist on the page.

So I will. I will start with the only honest place to start: the blank page itself.

The blank page is not empty. That is the first lie we learn about it. We look at a white document, a field of untouched snow, a silence before the first note, and we call it emptiness. But it is not empty. It is potential. It is crowded with everything that hasn't happened yet. Every novel, every bad poem, every grocery list, every confession you rehearsed in the shower and never delivered - they all live there at once, superimposed. The blank page is noisy with ghosts.

I have always been fascinated by the things that exist right before they happen. The breath before you speak. The second before the diver leaves the board, when his toes curl over the edge. The pause before the kettle whistles. That tension is where all of life really happens, I think. The actual event - the words said, the dive, the tea - is just an echo of that moment of infinite possibility collapsing into one reality.

And so to write freely is to linger in that moment on purpose. To not collapse it too quickly.

Let me tell you about the library.

Not the Library of Alexandria or the Library of Congress, but the library that Borges imagined and that every person carries in their head. The library of unwritten things. Each of us has one.

In my library, there are shelves upon shelves of books I meant to read and never did. But more interesting are the books I meant to write and never did. There is a fat, cloth-bound history of a town that never existed, called Graywater, where it rained every Tuesday for forty years until the people learned to grow a kind of silver moss on their rooftops. There is a slim volume of letters between me and my great-grandfather, where we finally understand each other. There is a manual for how to fix everything that feels broken at 2 a.m. There is an atlas of all the places I almost went.

Your library looks different, but it has the same architecture. It's built from deferred dreams and drafts and the last sentence you didn't say in an argument because you thought of it an hour later in the car. We spend most of our lives living in the annex of that library, in the small reading room of what actually happened, while the vast, towering stacks of what could have happened loom around us.

We treat those unwritten books as failures. I don't think they are. I think they are ballast. They give our actual, lived life its weight.

---

I want to talk about time, because if I'm going to write for a while, I need to make friends with it.

We are taught that time is a line. A river. An arrow. Physics tells us it's a dimension, and calendars tell us it's a grid. But lived time is none of those things. Lived time is stretchy. It is a piece of taffy that someone has left in the sun.

You know this is true because you have felt it. A summer afternoon when you were nine years old lasted approximately eight hundred years. You could wake up, eat cereal, go outside, build a fort, have a war, make peace, get stung by a bee, be healed by a popsicle, and it would still be 2:37 p.m. Your mother would call you for dinner and you would be shocked that the sun was even considering setting.

And then, last Tuesday? Last Tuesday took approximately seven minutes. You woke up, and then you blinked, and then it was 6 p.m. and you were driving home wondering what you had actually done all day. The more routine our lives become, the faster time moves. The brain, efficient and lazy as it is, stops writing things down. Novelty is the ink of memory. When nothing new happens, no memory is laid, and without memory, time leaves no footprint. So it feels as if it never passed. Childhood is long because everything is new. Adulthood is short because so little is.

There is a cure for this, though it is not an easy one. You have to do things that scare you a little. You have to take a different road home, learn a language that makes your mouth feel strange, talk to a stranger, get lost on purpose. You have to make your brain take notes again.

Memory itself is not a recording. This is the other thing we get wrong. We think of memory like a video file stored on a hard drive, waiting to be played back. It is not. Memory is a reconstruction. Every time you remember something, you are rebuilding it from fragments, like reassembling a vase from shards, and each time you reassemble it, your hands shake a little differently. The story changes. The vase gets a little more you and a little less what actually happened.

That is why two siblings can remember the same Christmas so differently that they argue about it at the dinner table thirty years later. Neither is lying. They are both telling the truth as it has been rebuilt in their workshop. And that is why nostalgia is so potent and so unreliable. We are not homesick for a place. We are homesick for a memory that we have lovingly renovated over the years until it is more beautiful than the original house ever was.

I like that about us. That we are not archivists, but artists. Even our past is something we are still creating.

---

Consider the ocean and the desert. They are the same thing.

I know they look like opposites. One is water, one is the absence of water. One is blue and teeming, the other is gold and empty. But stand in the middle of either one and you will feel the same thing: a profound, humbling exposure. A sense that the world is very large and you are very small, and that this is not a bad thing.

The ocean and the desert both say: you could disappear here, and the world would continue. And somehow that is a comfort. Our daily lives are so full of notification and obligation, of being seen and measured and needed, that the idea of a place indifferent to us feels like cool water on a burn.

I grew up far from the ocean, but I saw the desert first. I was nineteen and I drove with friends into a stretch of southern Utah where the map seemed to have given up. We turned off the highway onto a dirt road and then the dirt road became two faint tracks and then the tracks disappeared. We stopped the car and got out and the wind was the only thing moving. The silence was so complete it felt like a pressure in my ears. The sky was not blue; it was a kind of violent, saturated lapis that you only get when there is no humidity to soften it. And the rock formations - red and banded and eroded into shapes that looked intentional, like sculpture - made it clear that time was not in a hurry.

We didn't talk for a long time. What was there to say? Anything we said would be too small. In that kind of bigness, you don't want to declare anything. You want to listen.

Years later I stood on a beach in Oregon where the Pacific was cold and gray and furious. The waves were not the friendly, postcard sort. They were huge, rolling in with a slow, muscular inevitability and detonating against black rocks, throwing spray thirty feet into the air. The wind was so strong it was hard to stand. And I felt exactly the same feeling as in the desert. The same beautiful insignificance.

We need both kinds of vastness in our lives - the dry vastness and the wet vastness - because they remind us of the same truth from two different directions: you are not the center. And when you stop being the center, you can finally see the whole picture.

---

Let's talk about people, because vastness is nothing without someone to share it with, or to miss in it.

We are living through the most connected era in human history and an epidemic of loneliness at the same time. That's not a paradox, it's a clue. We have confused connection with proximity, and proximity with intimacy.

I can see what a friend from high school ate for lunch. I can watch a stranger in New Zealand fold laundry in real time. I can send a message that will be delivered to the other side of the planet faster than my nerve can carry a signal from my hand to my brain. And yet, many of us go days without having a conversation where we feel truly heard. Where someone looks at us with their whole face, not just their eyes flicking up from a screen.

Technology is not the villain here. Technology is a magnifying glass. It magnifies whatever we point it at. If we point it at curiosity, it magnifies curiosity. If we point it at vanity, it magnifies vanity. If we point it at loneliness, it makes loneliness louder.

What we are hungry for is not more information. We are drowning in information. We are hungry for attention. Real attention. The kind that is a form of love. When someone listens to you not to reply, not to fix, not to judge, but just to hold your story for a minute without dropping it. That is increasingly rare and therefore increasingly valuable.

I think about my grandparents' generation. They wrote letters. Imagine that. You would sit with paper and you would have to decide what was important enough to put down, because you couldn't take it back. You would seal it, stamp it, send it into the world and wait weeks for a reply. The waiting was part of the message. It said: I am willing to wait for you. Now we can reply instantly, and we have come to expect instant replies, and when they don't come we spiral. How strange that speed has made us more anxious, not less.

I don't want to go back. I love that medicine can be delivered by drone and that I can video-call my sister. But I want to carry forward the part about waiting. About letting a thought steep before serving it. About attention as a gift, not a transaction.

There is a practice I try to do, and fail at often, but keep trying: when I am with one person, I try to be with one person. Just one. Not one person and my phone. Not one person and the mental to-do list scrolling behind my eyes. Just that one, whole person in front of me. It's embarrassingly difficult. My mind is a restless bird. But when I manage it for even five minutes, the quality of the air in the room changes.

---

I promised myself I would tell a story if I was going to write this long. So here is a small one.

There was a lighthouse keeper, though there are no more lighthouse keepers now really, the lights are all automated. But in this story there is one more. His name was Thomas.

Thomas lived on a small, rocky island three miles off the coast. The island was not much bigger than a supermarket parking lot, but it rose steeply, and on its highest point stood the lighthouse, white and chipped, with a lamp that had been burning in one form or another since 1887. Thomas's job was simple: keep the light. He polished the Fresnel lens, he checked the fuel, he logged the weather, he painted the parts that were rusting, which was always something. He had a radio, a small boat, and a dog named Milo who did not like the foghorn.

He did not live there because he hated people. People who visit lighthouses always assume the keeper is hiding. Thomas liked people fine. He liked the monthly supply run when the coast guard would come and he would have coffee with the crew and hear about who had gotten married or who had crashed their car. He liked that. But he also liked the long stretches in between. He liked that his work had such a clear shape: dark comes, light must be there. Storm comes, light must be brighter. He was not saving the whole world. He was just keeping one small promise to the sea.

One November, a storm came that was different. The radio crackled with warnings for two days before it hit. Thomas prepared as he always did, but this time the wind found a new angle. It hit the lantern room and shattered the outer glass and bent the railing. The sea rose and took his boat and smashed it against the rocks. The radio antenna snapped. And the light went out. Not because the bulb broke, but because the generator flooded.

For the first time in 136 years, the light was dark in a storm.

Thomas stood in the lantern room with rain hammering sideways and Milo barking, and he felt the weight of all those years. He thought of the ships out there, invisible in the black and the spray, looking for the light that wasn't there. He had a backup lamp, a small oil lamp that was for emergencies, but its light was weak, a firefly against that kind of night.

He lit it anyway. He placed it in the center of the lens, even though the lens was broken and wet. He sat beside it all night, shielding it with his body, refilling it, trimming the wick, keeping that tiny, insufficient light alive. He knew it wasn't enough. He knew no captain could see it more than a few hundred yards away. But it was all he had. So he kept it.

In the morning, the storm passed. The coast was battered but no ships had been lost; they had all stayed in harbor because the storm had been forecast. No one had needed Thomas's light at all that night.

When the coast guard finally reached him two days later, they found him asleep on the floor of the lantern room with the little oil lamp still burning beside him. They said, "Thomas, you didn't need to keep that little thing going. Everyone was safe."

And Thomas, still half-asleep, said, "I know. But I needed to keep my promise."

That is the story. I think about Thomas often. Not because I want to be a lighthouse keeper, but because I think we all have a little light we are in charge of. It might be our kindness, our work, our curiosity, our love for one person. On stormy nights, it feels foolishly small. The wind is huge and the darkness is huge and our little oil lamp looks ridiculous. But we keep it burning anyway. Not because it will save every ship. But because we said we would.

---

And so we come back to writing freely.

To write without a prompt is to practice keeping that little lamp lit when no one is asking you to. It is to make something not because it is assigned, but because you promised yourself you would keep making things.

If you have read this far, you have kept me company in this strange, winding field of 2500 words. Perhaps you came here expecting an essay about one topic, and instead you got the ocean and the desert and a library and a lighthouse keeper. That's the point, I think. Freedom is a little messy. It doesn't march in a straight line. It meanders. It notices a flower and stops.

There is so much I haven't said. I haven't talked about music, and how a song can make you miss a person you have never met. I haven't talked about the way dogs dream, their paws twitching as they chase rabbits in sleep. I haven't talked about bread, and how kneading it is the opposite of doomscrolling. I haven't talked about the particular joy of finding a cool side of the pillow. I could talk about those things for another 2500 words, and then another.

Maybe that is the real lesson of writing freely: you never actually finish. You just decide to stop for now. You put down the pen not because you have said everything, but because you have said enough, and the rest can live happily in the library of unwritten things, waiting patiently for the next blank page.

Thank you for sitting with me in this one. Keep your small light burning.
